extracted.intended_audience: educated readers of natural philosophy, mathematicians/astronomers, and lay readers interested in natural theology (18th-century learned public)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and argumentation using astronomical and experimental observations to demonstrate natural theology (existence/attributes of a Creator) and to establish astronomical facts (e.g., Sun's magnitude, motions). Combines observational method, mathematical demonstration, and responses to sceptical objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove the Sun is bigger than the Earth by lunar eclipses
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the shape and tapering of the Earth's shadow on the Moon during eclipses (shadow forms a pyramidal/conical figure whose vertex lies beyond the Moon) to infer that the Sun's diameter is much larger than the Earth's.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine the shadow's diameter at the Moon's distance (shadow grows continually smaller from AZ to L making a pyramid ALZ); if Sun were smaller than Earth the shadow would not taper as observed. This geometric inference delivers a convincing proof independent of advanced optics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine Sun's magnitude from parallax and apparent diameter
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute the Sun's real semidiameter by measuring (1) the horizontal parallax (angle ACB) using the Earth's semidiameter as unit, and (2) the Sun's apparent semidiameter (angle DBC), then apply trigonometry/proportional reasoning to find the Sun's true semidiameter and thus its volume (cubic relation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As the Angle ACB (horizontal parallax) is to Angle DBC (apparent semidiameter), so is Earth's semidiameter AB to Sun's semidiameter DC. Modern measurement of parallax (seconds) and apparent diameter (minutes) yields numerical ratios; cubing semidiameters gives relative volumes. Note sensitivity: small changes in parallax produce large changes in computed solar volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple observational methods and convergence of results
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ different methods (ancient geometric observations, lunar-distance methods, telescopes with micrometers) to determine angles such as parallax and apparent diameter and prefer conclusions where methods converge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discrepancies among astronomers historically arose from instrument limits and methods; modern methods (telescopes + micrometers) reduce mistakes and produce values to seconds. Prefer results confirmed by independent, more exact methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rely on modern instruments (telescopes, micrometers, pendulum-clocks) for accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Give greater weight to observations made with telescopes armed with micrometers and accurate timing devices, because they reduce observational errors compared to ancient instruments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The parallax angle has shrunk as instruments improved (from minutes to seconds). Use telescopes and micrometers to observe small angles; pendulum clocks help make the firmament serve as a quadrant. Treat ancient minute-level observations as less exact than modern second-level ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical demonstration via triangles and trigonometry
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame astronomical distance and size problems as geometric/trigonometric problems (triangles with known side/angles) so that known sides/angles determine unknown distances/diameters with mathematical certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in triangle ABC, knowing semidiameter AB and parallax angle ACB allows computing distance BC; in triangle DBC, knowing BC and apparent semidiameter DBC gives Sun's semidiameter DC. When two angles and one side are known, trigonometry yields the rest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware taking hypotheses as truth—convenience ≠ reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume that a simpler or more convenient hypothesis (e.g., moving Earth vs. fixed Sun) is necessarily true; mathematicians often adopt hypotheses for calculational convenience rather than as assertions of physical reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many celebrated astronomers use contradictory hypotheses depending on convenience; the simplicity of an hypothesis is not a reliable indicator of its truth. Always seek empirical/experimental proof rather than aesthetic or pragmatic grounds alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require experimental/observational proof for motions (e.g., Earth's motion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not claim certainty about large-scale motions (Sun's or Earth's motion) in absence of solid experimental evidence such as stellar parallax; theoretical convenience or widely-held hypotheses are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because great mathematicians themselves have confessed uncertainty, and because no fixed experimental proof (like measurable parallax of fixed stars) has been produced, one should withhold decisive assertion on Earth's motion until such decisive observations exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess observational uncertainty by instrument/method precision
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating differing astronomical claims, consider the precision and susceptibility to error of the observational method and instruments used (e.g., ancient large instruments vs. modern telescopes with micrometers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variety of reported values (parallax, apparent diameters) trace back to instrument accuracy; prefer measurements with smaller systematic errors and those reproducible at high precision (seconds of arc).

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish hydrostatical laws by ordered experiments and many replications
rubrics_metrics.description: Found hydrostatical laws (pressure up/down, lateral pressure, pressure adaptation to height not breadth, oblique pressures, behavior of fluids in curve tubes, fountains, syphons) on a systematic order of experiments and extensive replication (hundreds or thousands of experiments if necessary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lay out the order of experiments, compare lateral vs perpendicular pressures by direct experiments, use controlled variations (different fluids, heights, breadths), and confirm paradoxes by many replications (the text cites 1200 experiments for a hydrostatic paradox).

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate chemical laws experimentally (acids/alkalis, salts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use concrete experiments to show the operations of acids and alkalis, effervescences, precipitation and dispersion of salts, and properties of substances like saltpeter, drawing conclusions only from reproducible experimental evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide multiple experiments (e.g., seven experiments for saltpeter abundance) and link observed chemical operations to broader arguments (e.g., order and preservation in nature as evidence of design).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use observed regularity, order, and laws in nature as arguments for a Creator
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat the large-scale order, exact laws, mutual adaptations (e.g., gravity, motions, properties of light and fluids) and the preservation of things as empirical grounds for inferring an intelligent Creator and Ruler of the universe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect 'convictions' from multiple domains (astronomy, optics, hydrostatics, chemistry, particle observations) and answer atheist objections by showing the improbability of such ordered laws arising from chance; supplement with scriptural texts as part of the apologetic strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address sceptical objections by reducing them to empirical/mathematical analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: When facing philosophical or theological objections (e.g., objections to the possibility of resurrection, or objections based on unknowns like Earth's motion), answer them by laying out clear empirical, geometric, or particle-level analyses that resolve apparent paradoxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, discuss visible vs. own body, particle divisibility, adhesion of particles, and how bodies may be reconstituted; show how natural-philosophical principles can neutralize objections rather than appealing solely to authority.
